fullText:
TO COMPETE AGAINST TEMU AND AMAZON, SPECIALIST SHEIN MUST EVOLVE

Shein is a specialist in cross-border, ultra-fast fashion ecommerce. 

It’s a great service. 

And it has scaled beautifully. Up to +170 countries. 

Phase 1 of Shein was a great success. 

But staying a specialized ecommerce business won’t be enough to compete against the ecommerce giants.

Think Amazon, Alibaba and Temu.

Here are my 5 questions for assessing the viability of a specialty ecommerce company against such giants.

1: Is the company sufficiently differentiated in the user experience?

2: Can the company compete and/or differentiate in logistics or infrastructure without ongoing spending?

3: Does the company have a strong competitive advantage in a circumscribed market? 

4: Is there a clear path to significant operational cash flow?

5: Has the company avoided markets and situations that are attractive or strategic for the major ecommerce companies?

Shein doesn’t have a big moat (Ques 3). No network effects. 

It is much smaller than the ecommerce giants (Ques 2). Cash flow matters. 

And the giants view cross-border and fashion as strategic priorities (Ques 5). That’s a big problem. 

My conclusion: Competition for Shein is going to get more intense going forward.

And competitive intensity usually hits margins.

Listen to my latest podcast for my strategic breakdown of Shein. And some ideas for next steps.

fullText:
One reason why we’re going to get uneven diffusion rates of agents is because different workflows in the enterprise are more or less aligned to continuous, uninterrupted computer work.

A big reason why agentic coding growth has gone completely vertical is because it’s a type of work where economic value is directly correlated with the output of solely digital information, and where the task size can in theory be unbounded in a single session. This means that as AI agents can do larger amounts of work at a time, and as model capability improves on this task type, they can directly be deployed at larger workloads near instantaneously.

Lots of work doesn’t natively have this property in how today’s workflows are designed. A sales rep needs a feedback loop with the customer before they can do additional work for a specific account, a lawyer needs to talk to the client, and a doctor needs to interact with a patient. So large agentic work will likely not look the same as it has in coding, at least by default.

Instead, in many of these domains, the agents will actually need to tie into a workflow that is reengineered for AI.

Matan Grinberg at Factory had a good way of thinking about this on the Training Data podcast: if everyone called in sick tomorrow, token usage would plummet because no one would be there to prompt them. This shows how early we are in agents running in the background for most processes; whereas this should be the majority of volume of agentic work in the future. 

In legal, it will be about processing every contract that comes in, in sales it will be agents that roam through customer records and figure out signals of when to better do outreach, in life sciences research it will be about swarms of agents reading through every test or all research.

To do that these business processes have to be wired up to support agents, as opposed to the vast amounts of manual work that we do today. 

This is the big opportunity right now, but it’s going to diffuse differently from something like agentic coding. Lots of change management, lots of data cleanup, lots of workflow reengineering, and more.

I talked to a founder today who's doing a software startup after two previous hardware startups. He's so much more relaxed that he seems a different person. Hardware is hard. It's at least possible now, but it's still hard.

The workforce participation rate couldn’t be dropping at a worse time. Those who are employed are relearning their jobs with AI and agents augmenting them for the first time.

The people who are out of the workforce right now aren’t developing the same capabilities or gaining experience. Soon, all jobs will require X years of experience with those capabilities.

People out of the workforce will be faced with two options when their bills force them to reenter the workforce:

1. Start all over again. Take an entry-level job that doesn’t pay enough to maintain their prior lifestyle.

2. Apply to roles at their old level and hope for a supply-demand imbalance that makes employers willing to hire and upskill them.

Long-term unemployment is a huge problem that we need to address now. Reskilling workers early and giving them a pipeline back into the workforce is always the cheapest solution. In five years, our options will be far more complex to implement.

fullText:
New research from Meta.

Agent harnesses are still mostly authored by hand.

This makes it hard to tune robust agent harnesses for long-horizon tasks.

In this new work, agents learn harness policies offline and deploy them to construct and update external harness state online during runtime task execution.

EvoHarness-RL learns that policy instead. Belief, Progress, and Experience are exposed as harness state the policy can act on.

Supervised harness fine-tuning teaches the action space, then cost-aware GRPO explores when to read, update, and consolidate during a long run. Qwen3-8B reaches 96.9% on ALFWorld.

Two dynamics come out of the training.

> Harness annealing means recurring harness-use patterns get absorbed into the model policy, and the agent shifts from frequent calls toward selective access.

> Harness evolution means progress updates and experience consolidation compress the workspace into a compact task-adaptive state.

This shows that long-horizon agents get more from a trainable coordination policy than from bigger tools or larger memories.
